name: Creating a Dictionary of Character-Count Pairs
description:
Construct a program that has a function which receives a string from the user and creates a dictionary that maps each character in the given string to its frequency, that is, how many times that character appears in the given string.
For example, if the given string is "book", the program creates the following dictionary:
b : 1
o : 2
k : 1

comments.content:
We need to first declare the function that receives a string and create a dictionary that maps each character in the given string to its frequency, that is, how many times that character appears in the given string. The given string is referred by variable s.

Note that all statements following the header line are indented.

We first need to define a dictionary referred by variable counts for storing the frequency of the characters in the given string. We initialize it with an empty dictionary by setting it to a pair of braces {}.

We need this dictionary to store key-value pairs where each key represents a character in the given string and the value that is mapped to that represents the frequency of that character in the given string.

We want to iterate over the characters in the given string and update the frequency of them each time that they appear in the string. We can use a for loop to iterate through the characters in the string.
This for loop assigns the name char to each of the characters in the given string in turn, from left to right, and then the statement in the loop body will be executed for each character.
Note that all statements inside the loop need to be indented with respect to the loop header.

To determine if the visited character already exists as the key in the dictionary, we employ the in operator to test membership. Because the in operator implicitly scans the keys in the dictionary looking for a match.
If the visited character already exists as the key in the dictionary, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.

When the visited character already exists as the key in the dictionary, we need to increment its value by 1. This way, the frequency of the visited character in the given string will be increased by 1.
The += operator adds 1 to the value of the dictionary entry that has the visited character as its key. Therefore, it is functionally equivalent to the statement counts[char] = counts[char] + 1.

If the above if test fails (i.e., when the visited character does not exist as the key in the dictionary), we need to add a new entry to the dictionary with the visited character as the key and 1 as its value.
The statement inside the body of this else statement is executed when the visited character does not exist as the key in the dictionary. Otherwise, the body of this else statement is skipped.

When the visited character does not exist as the key in the dictionary, we need to add it to the dictionary as a new key and set its value to 1. We set its value to 1 because this is the first occurrence of the character in the given string.

This statement prints to the default standard output stream the text "The character counts for" and the value of variable s.
The printed text shows the arguments of the print function separated by the default delimiter (i.e., single space character) and followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

To see the frequency of each character, we need to iterate over the keys in the dictionary and print the value that is mapped to each key. We can use a for loop to iterate through the keys in the dictionary.

This for loop assigns the name char to each of the keys in the dictionary in turn, from left to right, and then the statement in the loop body will be executed for each character.

Note that each key in the dictionary represents a character in the given string.
Note that all statements inside the loop need to be indented with respect to the loop header.

This statement prints to the default standard output stream the visited key in the dictionary, the string ":" and the value that is mapped to that key.
Each key represents a character in the given string and the value that is mapped to that represents the frequency of that character in the given string.
The printed text shows the arguments of the print function separated by the default delimiter (i.e., single space character) and followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

We need to read the string that the user enters. To read the user input from the command line, we use the input() function. This statement prints a text on the screen "Enter a string: ", then reads the text entered by the user.

The value that will be read is a string; we assign it to variable s.
This statement calls the create_dictionary function and passes the string that the user enters as its argument. Note that the function call must be done after the function is declared.
